segments.text: Every triangle has thousands of hidden centers, and the Encyclopedia of Triangle Centers begins right here at X one: the Incenter. Join the three interior angle bisectors of triangle A B C, and they concur at a single invariant point, the center of the unique inscribed circle tangent to all three sides.

segments.text: Unlike a sequential proof in Euclid, a triangle center is defined by its homogeneous coordinates, which have two direct geometric pictures. First, look at the Trilinear coordinates, alpha, beta, gamma. Drop perpendiculars from X one to sidelines B C, C A, and A B. Because all three perpendicular struts are radii of the same incircle, their lengths are identical, giving X one the simplest trilinear ratio of all: one, to one, to one.

segments.text: Second, look at the Barycentric coordinates, u, v, w. Join X one to vertices A, B, and C, partitioning the triangle into three shaded sub-triangles. Each sub-triangle has base a, b, or c, and the same height r, so their areas are in the exact ratio of the side lengths: a, to b, to c. Compare the three classic centers side by side: X one has equal perpendicular distances, one to one to one; the centroid X two has equal sub-triangle areas, one to one to one; and the symmedian point X six has distances proportional to the sides, and areas proportional to the squares of the sides. Across acute, right, Kepler, and Kimberling triangles, X one remains the invariant heart of the inscribed circle.
